deep.reconstruction:
This image is not a new page of text. The right-hand side is the marbled inside back cover (pastedown) of the memorandum booklet, with its clasps; there is no writing on it. The left-hand strip is the right edge of the previous leaf (p. 106), cut off by the binding. So the 'transcription' of this page is only a truncated duplicate of the previous page.

What is visible are household notes, with no mathematical derivation:

(a) Lengths in mm with labels: 824 mm 'f.S.', 885 'können werden', 1170 'ganze Br[eite]'. These are furniture or room measurements.

(b) 'Länge eines Stücks Tapete aus dem obern Mittelzimmer 9 m 200': a roll of wallpaper from the upper middle room is 9.200 m long. Gauss converts this to 377.2 Zoll = 31 Fuß 5.2 Zoll. Check: 31·12 + 5.2 = 377.2, which is correct. The implied inch is 9200/377.2 ≈ 24.39 mm (my computation). That is close to the Hanoverian/Calenberg Zoll (≈24.34 mm, which would give ≈378.0 Zoll), so his conversion factor or rounding was slightly different.

(c) 'Höhe des Saals in der alten Wohnung 2 m 980': the height of the hall in the old apartment.

(d) Body-height records in mm: '1718,75 Ego' (Gauss himself), '1714,25 W' (presumably his son Wilhelm), dated Aug 10, 1837.

(e) A table of the children's heights in metres. The columns dated 1818 Jan 24 and 1819 März 12 read 1.361, 1.257, 1.105, 0.923. Further down is 0.769, which the previous page assigns to Therese. The note '1826 Dec. 26: Ich 1705, Jos[eph] 1727' gives heights in mm.

The only arithmetic is a unit conversion (metres to Fuß/Zoll) and the recording of measurements.
errors: No real error. The conversion 377.2 Zoll = 31 Fuß 5.2 Zoll is internally consistent. Using the standard Hanoverian Zoll (≈24.34 mm), 9.2 m would be ≈378 Zoll rather than 377.2, so Gauss used a slightly different factor (≈24.39 mm per Zoll) or a different foot.
